'''''Lonicera japonica''''', known as '''Japanese honeysuckle'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> and '''golden-and-silver honeysuckle''',<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|title=English Names for Korean Native Plants|publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]]|year=2015|isbn=978-89-97450-98-5|location=Pocheon|pages=525|access-date=4 January 2017|via=[[Korea Forest Service]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|archive-date=25 May 2017}}</ref> is a species of [[honeysuckle]] native to East Asia, including many parts of China. It is often grown as an ornamental plant, but has become an [[invasive species]] in a number of countries. It is used in traditional Chinese medicine.

==Description==
''Lonicera japonica'' is a twining [[vine (botany)|vine]]<ref>{{Cite book|title=Dictionary of Plant Lore|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WAagnZNb0cAC|publisher=Academic Press|date=2007-05-02|isbn=9780080546025|language=en|first=D. C.|last=Watts}}</ref> able to climb up to {{convert|10|m|abbr=on}} high or more in [[tree]]s, with opposite, simple oval [[leaf|leaves]] {{convert|3|–|8|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|2|–|3|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad. When its stems are young, they are slightly red in color and may be fuzzy. Older stems are brown with peeling bark, and are often hollow on the inside.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web|url=https://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/plant-directory/lonicera-japonica/|title=''Lonicera japonica''|publisher= – University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants|access-date=2019-09-27|archive-date=2023-09-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230926024525/https://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/plant-directory/lonicera-japonica/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The [[flower]]s are double-tongued, opening white and fading to yellow, and sweetly vanilla scented. The [[fruit]], which is produced in fall,<ref name=":02"/> is a black spherical [[berry (botany)|berry]] {{convert|3|–|4|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} diameter containing a few [[seed]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://tai2.ntu.edu.tw/udth/bin/fot1.exe/browse?BID=4&page=744 |title=''Lonicera japonica'' |work=Flora of Taiwan |access-date=2006-06-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060718144651/http://tai2.ntu.edu.tw/udth/bin/fot1.exe/browse?bid=4&page=744 |archive-date=2006-07-18 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Chemistry ===
''Lonicera japonica'' leaves contain [[methyl caffeate]], 3,4-di-O-[[caffeoylquinic acid]], [[methyl]] 3,4-di-O-[[caffeoylquinic acid]], [[protocatechuic acid]], methyl [[chlorogenic acid]], and [[luteolin]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Neeraj |last2=Singh |first2=Bikram |last3=Bhandari |first3=Pamita |last4=Gupta |first4=Ajai P. |last5=Uniyal |first5=Sanjay K. |last6=Kaul |first6=Vijay K. |year=2005 |title=Biflavonoids from ''Lonicera japonica'' |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=66 |issue=23 |pages=2740–4 |bibcode=2005PChem..66.2740K |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2005.10.002 |pmid=16293275}}</ref> Other [[polyphenol]]s present in the plant are [[hyperoside]] and [[caffeic acid]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peng |first1=Youyuan |last2=Liu |first2=Fanghua |last3=Ye |first3=Jiannong |year=2005 |title=Determination of Phenolic Acids and Flavones in ''Lonicera'' japonica Thumb. By Capillary Electrophoresis with Electrochemical Detection |journal=Electroanalysis |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=356 |doi=10.1002/elan.200403102}}</ref> The two secoiridoid glycosides, loniceracetalides A and B, can be isolated, together with 10 known iridoid glycosides, from the flower buds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kakuda |first1=Rie |last2=Imai |first2=Mio |last3=Yaoita |first3=Yasunori |last4=Machida |first4=Koichi |last5=Kikuchi |first5=Masao |year=2000 |title=Secoiridoid glycosides from the flower buds of ''Lonicera japonica'' |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=55 |issue=8 |pages=879–81 |bibcode=2000PChem..55..879K |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)00279-X |pmid=11140518}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The flowers can also be a significant source of food for deer, rabbits, hummingbirds, and other wildlife.<ref>''Forest Plants of the Southeast and Their Wildlife Uses'', James H. Miller and Karl V. Miller, University of Georgia Press, Revised Ed. 2005, p.278</ref>

=== As an invasive species ===
Japanese honeysuckle has become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, New Zealand, and much of the United States, including Hawaii, as well as a number of Pacific and Caribbean islands. It is classified as a noxious weed in 46 states, being prohibited to be bought and sold in Connecticut, Illinois, Massachusetts, and Vermont, and banned in Indiana and New Hampshire.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japanese honeysuckle |url=https://tsusinvasives.org/home/database/lonicera-japonica |access-date=2024-06-21 |publisher=Texas Invasive Species Institute}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Terrestrial Invasive Species - Plants |url=https://www.in.gov/dnr/6351.htm |publisher=[[Indiana Department of Natural Resources]] |access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref> It is on the [[New Hampshire]] invasive species list.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prohibited Invasive Plant Species Rules |url=https://www.agriculture.nh.gov/publications-forms/documents/prohibited-invasive-species.pdf |publisher=[[New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets, and Food]] |access-date=2019-11-09}}</ref>

''Lonicera japonica'' was initially brought to the U.S. from Japan in the early 1800s as an ornamental plant. It is still deliberately planted in the U.S. for reasons such as erosion control or forage for deer, but has become invasive in many areas.<ref name=":02" /> It prefers to invade areas that have been disturbed, such as roadsides or floodplains. It will generally only invade forests when the canopy has been opened by logging or fallen trees, as it grows less vigorously in the shade.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Maine Natural Areas Program, Invasive Plants, Japanese Honeysuckle |url=https://www.maine.gov/dacf/mnap/features/invasive_plants/lonicera_japonica.htm |publisher=Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry |access-date=2019-09-27}}</ref> Once it has invaded an area, ''Lonicera japonica'' grows rapidly and outcompetes native plants for sunlight and nutrients.<ref name=":02" /> It proliferates using both [[Sexual reproduction|sexual]] and [[vegetative reproduction]], producing seeds that are spread by animals and expanding locally via [[rhizome]]s.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=''Lonicera japonica'' Japanese honeysuckle |url=http://www.texasinvasives.org/plant_database/detail.php?symbol=LOJA |publisher=Texas Invasive Species Institute}}</ref> Eventually, it will form a dense thicket which prevents other plant species from germinating in that area.<ref name=":02" /> Due to its suppression of germination in the understory, ''Lonicera japonica'' also prevents the regeneration of trees.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Species: ''Lonicera japonica'' |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/vine/lonjap/all.html |work=Fire Effects Information System (FEIS) |publisher=[[United States Forest Service]] |access-date=2019-10-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820105223/https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/vine/lonjap/all.html |archive-date=20 August 2019}}</ref>
[[File:Lonicera japonica kz5.jpg|alt=A large patch of Japanese honeysuckle is growing on top of other plants.|thumb|''Lonicera japonica''<nowiki/>'s rapid growth allows it to outcompete other plants in the areas it invades.]]
Management of invasive ''Lonicera japonica'' has been achieved through a variety of means. Small patches can be removed by hand, or using simple digging tools,<ref name=":1" /> but all plant parts including roots and rhizomes must be removed to prevent resprouting.<ref name=":02" /> Larger patches can be removed through repeated mowing, but application of herbicide is also recommended to prevent regrowth.<ref name=":1" /> There has been some study of using [[controlled burn]]s to remove ''L. japonica'', but the underground portion of the plant is usually able to survive and resprout, limiting the effectiveness of this method.<ref name=":02" /> Browsing by herbivores may limit its growth, but is unlikely to eliminate it.<ref name=":2" />

==== Biological control ====
The EPA of New Zealand approved the release of ''[[Limenitis glorifica]]'' butterflies in 2013 as a [[Biological pest control|biological control]] for ''Lonicera japonica.'' This butterfly is host specific for Japanese honeysuckle, but it may incidentally feed on other closely related plants, including Himalayan honeysuckle ''[[Leycesteria formosa]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.epa.govt.nz/assets/FileAPI/hsno-ar/APP201710/0fbd280326/APP201710-APP201710-EPA-Advice-Document-FINAL.pdf |title= Import and release of ''Limenitis glorifica''|access-date=2024-06-08 |publisher=[[Environmental Protection Authority (New Zealand)]]}}</ref> ''[[Oberea shirahatai]]'' is a Japanese honeysuckle host-specific beetle that feeds on the stems and leaves of Japanese honeysuckle. It was released in New Zealand in 2018 as another ''L. japonica''-specialist biological control.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japanese honeysuckle stem beetle |url=https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/discover-our-research/biodiversity-biosecurity/weed-biocontrol/projects-agents/biocontrol-agents/japanese-honeysuckle-stem-beetle/ |publisher=Manaaki Whenua / Landcare Research |access-date=2024-06-08}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Even though it is a highly invasive and destructive plant,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.invasive.org/alien/pubs/midatlantic/loja.htm |title=Japanese Honeysuckle (''Lonicera japonica'') |work=Weeds Gone Wild: Alien Plant Invaders of Natural Areas}}</ref> this species is often sold by American nurseries as the [[cultivar]] 'Hall's Prolific' (''Lonicera japonica'' var. ''halliana''),{{citation needed|date=July 2018}} and in the UK as the cultivar 'Halliana'. The cultivar is also known as Hall's Japanese honeysuckle.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Lonicera japonica'' 'Halliana' |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]] |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/93277/Lonicera-japonica-Halliana/Details |access-date=13 July 2018}}</ref> It is an effective [[groundcover]] and has strong-smelling flowers. It can be cultivated by [[seed]], [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]], or [[layering (horticulture)|layering]]. In addition, it will spread itself via [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s if given enough space to grow. The variety ''L. japonica'' var. ''repens''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1188|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224041156/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1188|url-status=dead|archive-date=24 December 2012|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Lonicera japonica'' var. ''repens'' |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]]|access-date=22 May 2013}}</ref> has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|title=AGM Plants – Ornamental|date=July 2017|publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]]|page=61|access-date=25 March 2018}}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
All parts of the plant other than the flower nectar have the potential to be toxic if consumed in a very large quantity for its [[saponin]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Lonicera japonica'' (Hall's Honeysuckle, Japanese Honeysuckle) |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/lonicera-japonica/ |work=Gardener Plant Toolbox |publisher=[[North Carolina Extension]]|access-date=2019-11-09}}</ref>

==Uses==
Japanese honeysuckle flowers are edible to humans and appreciated for their sweet-tasting nectar. {{Citation needed|date=September 2024}}

===Herbal medicine===
In [[traditional Chinese medicine]],<ref name="Shang">{{cite journal |author1=Shang, X. |author2=Pan, H. |author3=Li, M. |author4=Miao, X. |author5=Ding, H. |year=2011 |title=''Lonicera japonica'' Thunb.: Ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry and pharmacology of an important traditional Chinese medicine |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=138 |issue=1 |pages=1–21 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2011.08.016 |pmid=21864666|pmc=7127058 }}</ref>  ''Lonicera japonica'' is called ''rěn dōng téng'' ({{wt|zh|忍冬}}{{wt|zh|藤}});<ref name="Shang" /> literally "winter enduring vine") or ''jīn yín huā''<ref name="Shang" /> ({{lang-zh|c=[[wiktionary:金|金]][[wiktionary:銀|銀]][[wiktionary:花|花]]}}; literally "gold-silver flower", in reference to the presence of flowers of different age on the same plant as each flower changes from white (silver) to yellow (gold)).{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}} Alternative Chinese names include ''er hua'' (二花) and ''shuang hua'' (雙花), meaning ''double-[color] flowers''.<ref>''Chinese Medical Herbology and Pharmacology'', John and Tina Chen, Art of Medicine Press, 1st ed. 2001, p. 171</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bensky |first1=Dan |last2=Barolet |first2=Randall |title=Chinese Herbal Medicine Formulas & Strategies |edition=2nd |publisher=Eastland Press |page=44 }}</ref>
